title: Writing down the answer
blurb: The talker writes only the final answer, copying where the thinker points. Today it is a small stand-in. The talker that writes English is a placeholder.

scenes.heading: Where we are: the talker writes the answer

caption.text: This is the last stop on the map: the talker.
Its only job is to write the final answer. It adds no thinking.
It reads the thinker's final state, and may copy from the question and the calculator's replies.
But only where the thinker points. Today's talker is a small stand-in.

scenes.heading: Three ways the talker writes, today

caption.text: Today's talker is a small stand-in with three ways to write an answer.
Span copy takes a stretch of letters from the question or a reply.
A word pointer takes one whole word from the question.
Letter slots spell the answer when it is not in the text.

scenes.heading: Span copy: a pointer, a step left, a stop

caption.text: The thinker's final state sets a pointer on the last digit of the last reply: the 0.
The copy steps one letter left and takes the 1.
Next to the left is a space. A learned stop head says stop.
The digits came out last first, 0 then 1. Plain code flips them to read 10.

scenes.heading: Span copy: how often, and what is hand code

caption.text: On every trained copy of the T1SDR model at 3M, span copy wrote 91.5% of the answers.
That counts how often it was used, not how often it was right.
The pointer and the stop head are learned. Three small pieces are still hand-written code.
The plan: one learned writer replaces them. That build has not been run.

scenes.heading: Letter slots: spelling an answer

caption.text: When the answer is not in the text, the talker spells it in letter slots.
There are 9 places: room for 8 letters and an end mark. Each place picks a letter, or copies one.
They fill last letter first, so yes comes out as s, e, y. The code flips it.

scenes.heading: The 8-letter limit, and the 35-letter path

caption.text: Today's answer slots hold 8 letters. A longer training answer would be cut to 8.
That never happened: 0 of 200,000 training answers were longer than 8.
But a fill-in blank of 9 to 12 letters would hit it.
The new build, B3, writes up to 35 letters and counts longer answers, never cutting them.
A count above 0 fails its sealed mark. Blanks of 9 to 12 letters are safe only here.

scenes.heading: The planned English talker is not built

caption.text: The finished plan has a real talker, about 25M numbers, that writes English.
It is not built. As built, the whole model is 373.1M: 271.0M of borrowed, frozen Gemma plus 102.1M trained.
How it would learn to write English is not in the plan. A separate team session owns that.

scenes.heading: Older tests of talking English

caption.text: These tests are older, from a design built on borrowed language models. Not today's talker.
A 350M model as reader and talker scored 66.1. The 1.2B system scored 92.6.
A small copy talker scored 13.6 on question kinds it never practised. The language-model talker scored 78.2.

scenes.heading: Web text teaches reading, not writing

caption.text: Free web text, called FineWeb-Edu, enters practice as fill-in-the-blank rows.
One word of 3 to 12 letters is hidden, and the model must name it.
So the run teaches reading English, not writing it.
By plan, 84% of the big run's practice text is web text.

scenes.heading: What would have to be true to win the race

caption.text: The plan's final proof is a race against small public models, such as SmolLM2-360M.
To win, it must be ahead by at least 3 points on our sealed tests, and ahead on a question set called bAbI.
The whole size is counted, borrowed numbers too. The race needs the English talker, which does not exist yet.
